**Neville Gruzman**, [AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Member of the Order of Australia") (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"), mayor of [Woollahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Woollahra "Municipality of Woollahra"), [writer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing "Writing") and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney")'s architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Gruzman was born in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, [Bellevue Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hill,_New_South_Wales "Bellevue Hill, New South Wales"), exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from [Sydney Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Boys_High_School "Sydney Boys High School").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)

In the late 1940s Neville entered the [University of Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney "University of Sydney"), where [Beaux Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European [Modernists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture"), who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the [School of Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney_School_of_Architecture,_Design_and_Planning "University of Sydney School of Architecture, Design and Planning") in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with [Bill and Ruth Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_and_Ruth_Lucas "Bill and Ruth Lucas"). He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lloyd_Wright "Frank Lloyd Wright"). His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then [Object: Australian Design Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object:_Australian_Design_Centre "Object: Australian Design Centre").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.

Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Architecture")]

Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of [Modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") known as Organic Modernism, or [Regionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalism_(art) "Regionalism (art)"); some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional [post and beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_and_lintel "Post and lintel") architecture he saw at places like [Katsura Imperial Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsura_Imperial_Villa "Katsura Imperial Villa")—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, [Middle Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Cove,_New_South_Wales "Middle Cove, New South Wales")). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."

Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)

Gruzman is loosely connected to the [Sydney School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_School "Sydney School") of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the [International Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_style_(architecture) "International style (architecture)") of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.

## Notable projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notable projects")]

**Montrose Apartments** — [Neutral Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutral_Bay "Neutral Bay"), New South Wales (1954–1955)

Located at 445 Alfred Street, Neutral Bay, this lightweight glass and steel block of eight double-storey apartments was designed by Gruzman in his first year of practice. The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)

Montrose Apartments (1954–55), [Neutral Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutral_Bay "Neutral Bay") in March 2018

**Hills House** — [Turramurra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turramurra "Turramurra"), New South Wales (1966, 1983)

Original client was Sam Rosenburg, a nudist and vegetarian. Gruzman's idea was to build a series of hills that surround the site on three sides making it visually and acoustically private. Later, expansion was added for new clients, a family with three children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) The building is referred to by [Philip Goad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Goad "Philip Goad") as a product of two iconic 20th-century houses (Wright's [Fallingwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallingwater "Fallingwater") and [Mies van der Rohe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Mies_van_der_Rohe "Ludwig Mies van der Rohe")[Farnsworth House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnsworth_House_(Plano,_Illinois) "Farnsworth House (Plano, Illinois)")) that created the ultimate diagram of abstract shelter in the landscape.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/85/Gruzman_house.jpg/250px-Gruzman_house.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gruzman_house.jpg)

Gruzman House (1958–65), [Darling Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling_Point "Darling Point")

**Gruzman House** — [Darling Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling_Point "Darling Point"), New South Wales (1958, 1965, 1995)

Gruzman's own house built for his family is a hidden sanctuary, entirely private and distant from noise, is located at 4 Oswald Street not far from the busy New South Head Road.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-14) The living area was joyous, with its classical organic interior embellished with a collection of paintings, sculpture, and porcelain.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)[Jørn Utzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B8rn_Utzon "Jørn Utzon") judged that the house possessed the best [living room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_room "Living room") in Australia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-lawson-15) Another focus point is Gruzman's wife's dressing room with infinite light reflections from the mirrors on the walls on all four sides and on the ceiling.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-lawson-15) The house was extended in 1963 and again in the early 1990s.

**Goodman House** — [Middle Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Cove,_New_South_Wales "Middle Cove, New South Wales"), New South Wales (1956–57, 1983)

Designed for a couple soon after Gruzman's Japan trip, ideas of traditional Japanese architecture are infused in the design. Such as the entry to the [pagoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pagoda "Pagoda")-like end of the house and a sweeping curved roof suspended by cables.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-16) It is one of the early houses in Sydney to use materials such as dark stained timbers and natural [brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick "Brick").The house is located at The Quarterdeck, 17 North Arm Road.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)

**Gaden House (Mixed Use Office Building)** — [Double Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Bay "Double Bay"), New South Wales (1968–71)

A modernist three storey commercial building with a lower ground level located at the corner of Bay Street and Cooper Street, Double Bay (2a Cooper Street). It was designed in 1968, development application lodged on 18 March 1969 and later opened by NSW Premier [Robert Askin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Askin "Robert Askin") on 25 November 1971. The building was designed for solicitors, Gaden, Bowen and Stewart, who occupied the first floor, and office space for lease on the second floor, eight shops on the ground floor and a large restaurant in the lower ground floor called D'Arcys. In a 2018 heritage assessment Anne Warr described how the project _"... challenged the status quo of suburban shopping centres and transformed what could have been an ordinary suburban office and retail building into a work of art, pushing the design boundaries to produce a building that was a sculpture, both as an object in the streetscape at night as well as during the day, and in the interiors as a delightful and environmentally comfortable place to work."_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-17) In 2018 a development application was made for major changes to the building. A petition from local architects and the community was established to raise the plight of the building.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-18) The application was rejected by Woollahra Council. In 2020 the building was sold, and a new development application prepared that preserved the original Gruzman design.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-19) The new development application was prepared by architects Lawton Hurley and approved in 2022.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-20)

**Gowing House** — [Castlecrag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlecrag "Castlecrag"), New South Wales (1969)

An application for a house at 8A The Bulwark for J. Gowing was prepared by Gruzman Architects, Town Planners and Landscape Architects, with Wargon Chapman and Associates Engineers in February 1970. Plans for a two-storey house were amended to a single storey after Gowing suffered a stroke in 1973. The Heritage Study for Willougby City Council describes the dwelling's value and heritage listing _"Comparison of the Gowing House with other Gruzman houses highlights the individuality of the design solution for each project, key aspects of Gruzman’s work are evident in this house notably the responsiveness to the site, a carefully considered spatial flow with thought to privacy and light, exquisite detailing, and a touch of ‘Hollywood glamour’"_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-21)

## Political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Political career")]

In the 1980s Gruzman joined the Anti-Wall Committee formed to protect the [Sydney Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House "Sydney Opera House") from nearby urban development.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-24) In 1997 he chaired the renamed "Save East Circular Quay Committee".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-25)

In the 1990s Gruzman became politically active and was elected first as a councilor and then mayor of [Woollahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Woollahra "Municipality of Woollahra"), on a platform of responsible urban development. He was a critic of urban planning in Sydney, and also Sydney architects, notably [Harry Seidler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler "Harry Seidler"). Both his architectural criticism and time as mayor were controversial.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)

## Career as a teacher

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Career as a teacher")]

Gruzman began teaching at the [University of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_New_South_Wales "University of New South Wales") in the 1960s with a number of contemporary modernist architects such as [Bill Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Lucas_(architect) "Bill Lucas (architect)") and [Harry Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Howard_(landscape_architect) "Harry Howard (landscape architect)"). He became an adjunct professor and, as a critic of shortening teaching hours and increasing class size, was known for using Saturdays and public holidays to give extra classes to his students at his own home. In 2002 he established two student awards at the Faculty of the [Built Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built_Environment "Built Environment"), both for the best use of [urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design") in architecture. In his studio practise, beginning from the 1950s, he also employed and trained many notable Sydney architects, including [Pritzker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_Prize "Pritzker Prize") winner [Glenn Murcutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Murcutt "Glenn Murcutt").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-keulemans-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-28)

## Portrait and memoirs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Portrait and memoirs")]

In 1970, Gruzman was the subject of the winning entry for the [Archibald Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize"), painted by [Eric Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Smith_(artist) "Eric Smith (artist)").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-29) Gruzman sat for Smith several times, and commissioned Smith to contribute mosaics and stained glass for buildings he designed, including the South Head and District Synagogue in Rose Bay, as well as paintings Smith produced for the houses of his clients.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-31) Eric Smith later painted Gruzman's client and gallery owner [Rudy Komon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Komon "Rudy Komon") in 1981, again winning the [Archibald Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-32)

Most of Gruzman's houses were photographed by [Max Dupain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Dupain "Max Dupain") and [David Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moore_(Australian_photographer) "David Moore (Australian photographer)").

Gruzman's memoirs, incorporated into a book written by [Philip Goad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Goad "Philip Goad") and featuring many of the Dupain and Moore photographs, was published posthumously in 2006 by Craftsman House.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-33)

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Honours")]

An exhibition of Gruzman's work was held at the [RAIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Institute_of_Architects "Australian Institute of Architects") NSW Chapter in 1983, and a retrospective was held in 1992 at the Rex Irwin Gallery in Sydney.

Gruzman was appointed a [Member of the Order of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Member of the Order of Australia") (AM) in the 1985 Australia Day Honours.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-34)

The _Margot and Neville Gruzman Award for Urban Design in Architecture_ was named after Gruzman acknowledging his commitment to teaching of architecture and urban design at the [University of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_New_South_Wales "University of New South Wales"). The award is given to the best fourth year student, and an award for best final year architecture student whose design studio project best recognises the importance of urban design in architecture.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-keulemans-27)

**Neville Gruzman**, [AM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Member of the Order of Australia") (14 November 1925—1 May 2005) was an Australian [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"), mayor of [Woollahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Woollahra "Municipality of Woollahra"), [writer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing "Writing") and architectural activist. He is considered to have exerted a decisive influence on [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney")'s architecture, mostly through his dedication to designing architecture that reacts to the landscape and to the needs of the client.

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Gruzman was born in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), Australia. His parents—Sam Gruzman and Rosalind Gunzburg—were of Russian origin. He was the middle son, with Laurence, the eldest and Des, the youngest. His childhood near Cooper Park, [Bellevue Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellevue_Hill,_New_South_Wales "Bellevue Hill, New South Wales"), exerted a certain influence on him regarding his attitude towards landscape. He initially intended to fulfill his mother's wish to study medicine but enrolled for architecture after graduating from [Sydney Boys High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Boys_High_School "Sydney Boys High School").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1) His brother Laurence studied Law and became a barrister and later Queen's Counsel in 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-2)

In the late 1940s Neville entered the [University of Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney "University of Sydney"), where [Beaux Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaux-Arts_architecture "Beaux-Arts architecture") was a main subject. The first three years of his studyings were difficult for him as he wasn't good in drawing. However, he profited from his work experiences. He developed an interest in ballrooms, particularly mirrors and reflections, and won some skills with glamorous decoration from an interior decorator, Margaret Jaye. In his fourth year at university, he was attracted to the European [Modernists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture"), who influenced and furthered him. Before he graduated, he designed the _Lapin House_, Rose Bay for his aunt. He graduated from the [School of Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Sydney_School_of_Architecture,_Design_and_Planning "University of Sydney School of Architecture, Design and Planning") in 1952 and traveled to Europe with other graduates. Returning to Australia, he opened an office with [Bill and Ruth Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_and_Ruth_Lucas "Bill and Ruth Lucas"). He read the work _Architectural Beauty in Japan_. He later travelled to Japan on a four-and-a-half month study visit — a journey that would be followed by numerous others to the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) Later, Gruzman was amazed by the work of [Frank Lloyd Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Lloyd_Wright "Frank Lloyd Wright"). His understanding of the aspects of planning and of the necessities of an ongoing development grew decisively, in this period. His interests in creative arts extended to craft and in 1964 he founded the Craft Association, Australia's first such entity, later renamed the Crafts Council of NSW[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-4) and then [Object: Australian Design Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Object:_Australian_Design_Centre "Object: Australian Design Centre").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-5) In about 1967, he devoted himself to teaching; he is reported to have reassured his students attended the classes, regularly, and to have renounced holidays to provide extra tutorials for his students.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6) He also participated in politics, to improve the quality of built environment.

Gruzman had poor health. He suffered from asthma and heart attacks but managed to recover. He also had an accident that led to brain surgery causing the loss of most of his memory, including for details such as door dimensions, which he most attentively relearned.

## Architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Architecture")]

Gruzman mostly built residential houses in Sydney. His works are varied forms of [Modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") known as Organic Modernism, or [Regionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regionalism_(art) "Regionalism (art)"); some show a strong influence by the works of Frank Lloyd Wright. The impressions exerted on him on his trips to Japan—mainly by the traditional [post and beam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post_and_lintel "Post and lintel") architecture he saw at places like [Katsura Imperial Villa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katsura_Imperial_Villa "Katsura Imperial Villa")—influenced some of the homes he created and into which he eventually included Japanese elements[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-7) (_Goodman House_, [Middle Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Cove,_New_South_Wales "Middle Cove, New South Wales")). In the 1960s Gruzman gained recognition for private homes built for wealthy and sometimes eccentric clients along Sydney's north shore, such as the _Hill's House_ (1966), designed for a nudist[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-8) and the "theatrical" _Holland House_ (1962),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-9) built for an actress, who would both delight and scare her guests by dancing on the house's handrail-less balcony hanging over a cliff face. His work has been described as "major gestures, very Hollywood glamour."

Gruzman's architectural principles included maximum exposure to sunlight and privacy visually and audibly.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-10)

Gruzman is loosely connected to the [Sydney School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_School "Sydney School") of architects of the 1950s and 1960s[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-11)—a movement that started in opposition to the [International Style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_style_(architecture) "International style (architecture)") of modernism supported by other Australian architects and that has recently been re-discovered by home buyers and architectural fans, leading to a trend to preserve the homes from the period.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-12) However, Gruzman's work deviates from the Sydney School style in important traits; Gruzman himself denied a connection to the movement.

## Notable projects

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Notable projects")]

**Montrose Apartments** — [Neutral Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutral_Bay "Neutral Bay"), New South Wales (1954–1955)

Located at 445 Alfred Street, Neutral Bay, this lightweight glass and steel block of eight double-storey apartments was designed by Gruzman in his first year of practice. The building was highly innovative in its planning and visual impact in the landscape. It is a very early example of modernist residential curtain wall construction in Australia.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-13)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/Montrose_Apartments_exterior.jpg/250px-Montrose_Apartments_exterior.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Montrose_Apartments_exterior.jpg)

Montrose Apartments (1954–55), [Neutral Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutral_Bay "Neutral Bay") in March 2018

**Hills House** — [Turramurra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turramurra "Turramurra"), New South Wales (1966, 1983)

Original client was Sam Rosenburg, a nudist and vegetarian. Gruzman's idea was to build a series of hills that surround the site on three sides making it visually and acoustically private. Later, expansion was added for new clients, a family with three children.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-mccartney-3) The building is referred to by [Philip Goad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Goad "Philip Goad") as a product of two iconic 20th-century houses (Wright's [Fallingwater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallingwater "Fallingwater") and [Mies van der Rohe's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_Mies_van_der_Rohe "Ludwig Mies van der Rohe")[Farnsworth House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farnsworth_House_(Plano,_Illinois) "Farnsworth House (Plano, Illinois)")) that created the ultimate diagram of abstract shelter in the landscape.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/8/85/Gruzman_house.jpg/250px-Gruzman_house.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gruzman_house.jpg)

Gruzman House (1958–65), [Darling Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling_Point "Darling Point")

**Gruzman House** — [Darling Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darling_Point "Darling Point"), New South Wales (1958, 1965, 1995)

Gruzman's own house built for his family is a hidden sanctuary, entirely private and distant from noise, is located at 4 Oswald Street not far from the busy New South Head Road.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-14) The living area was joyous, with its classical organic interior embellished with a collection of paintings, sculpture, and porcelain.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)[Jørn Utzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J%C3%B8rn_Utzon "Jørn Utzon") judged that the house possessed the best [living room](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Living_room "Living room") in Australia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-lawson-15) Another focus point is Gruzman's wife's dressing room with infinite light reflections from the mirrors on the walls on all four sides and on the ceiling.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-lawson-15) The house was extended in 1963 and again in the early 1990s.

**Goodman House** — [Middle Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Cove,_New_South_Wales "Middle Cove, New South Wales"), New South Wales (1956–57, 1983)

Designed for a couple soon after Gruzman's Japan trip, ideas of traditional Japanese architecture are infused in the design. Such as the entry to the [pagoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pagoda "Pagoda")-like end of the house and a sweeping curved roof suspended by cables.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-16) It is one of the early houses in Sydney to use materials such as dark stained timbers and natural [brick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick "Brick").The house is located at The Quarterdeck, 17 North Arm Road.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goad-1)

**Gaden House (Mixed Use Office Building)** — [Double Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_Bay "Double Bay"), New South Wales (1968–71)

A modernist three storey commercial building with a lower ground level located at the corner of Bay Street and Cooper Street, Double Bay (2a Cooper Street). It was designed in 1968, development application lodged on 18 March 1969 and later opened by NSW Premier [Robert Askin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Askin "Robert Askin") on 25 November 1971. The building was designed for solicitors, Gaden, Bowen and Stewart, who occupied the first floor, and office space for lease on the second floor, eight shops on the ground floor and a large restaurant in the lower ground floor called D'Arcys. In a 2018 heritage assessment Anne Warr described how the project _"... challenged the status quo of suburban shopping centres and transformed what could have been an ordinary suburban office and retail building into a work of art, pushing the design boundaries to produce a building that was a sculpture, both as an object in the streetscape at night as well as during the day, and in the interiors as a delightful and environmentally comfortable place to work."_[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-17) In 2018 a development application was made for major changes to the building. A petition from local architects and the community was established to raise the plight of the building.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-18) The application was rejected by Woollahra Council. In 2020 the building was sold, and a new development application prepared that preserved the original Gruzman design.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-19) The new development application was prepared by architects Lawton Hurley and approved in 2022.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-20)

**Gowing House** — [Castlecrag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castlecrag "Castlecrag"), New South Wales (1969)

An application for a house at 8A The Bulwark for J. Gowing was prepared by Gruzman Architects, Town Planners and Landscape Architects, with Wargon Chapman and Associates Engineers in February 1970. Plans for a two-storey house were amended to a single storey after Gowing suffered a stroke in 1973. The Heritage Study for Willougby City Council describes the dwelling's value and heritage listing _"Comparison of the Gowing House with other Gruzman houses highlights the individuality of the design solution for each project, key aspects of Gruzman’s work are evident in this house notably the responsiveness to the site, a carefully considered spatial flow with thought to privacy and light, exquisite detailing, and a touch of ‘Hollywood glamour’"_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-21)

## Political career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Political career")]

In the 1980s Gruzman joined the Anti-Wall Committee formed to protect the [Sydney Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House "Sydney Opera House") from nearby urban development.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-24) In 1997 he chaired the renamed "Save East Circular Quay Committee".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-25)

In the 1990s Gruzman became politically active and was elected first as a councilor and then mayor of [Woollahra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipality_of_Woollahra "Municipality of Woollahra"), on a platform of responsible urban development. He was a critic of urban planning in Sydney, and also Sydney architects, notably [Harry Seidler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Seidler "Harry Seidler"). Both his architectural criticism and time as mayor were controversial.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)

## Career as a teacher

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Career as a teacher")]

Gruzman began teaching at the [University of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_New_South_Wales "University of New South Wales") in the 1960s with a number of contemporary modernist architects such as [Bill Lucas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Lucas_(architect) "Bill Lucas (architect)") and [Harry Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Howard_(landscape_architect) "Harry Howard (landscape architect)"). He became an adjunct professor and, as a critic of shortening teaching hours and increasing class size, was known for using Saturdays and public holidays to give extra classes to his students at his own home. In 2002 he established two student awards at the Faculty of the [Built Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Built_Environment "Built Environment"), both for the best use of [urban design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_design "Urban design") in architecture. In his studio practise, beginning from the 1950s, he also employed and trained many notable Sydney architects, including [Pritzker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pritzker_Prize "Pritzker Prize") winner [Glenn Murcutt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Murcutt "Glenn Murcutt").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-goadobituary-6)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-keulemans-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-28)

## Portrait and memoirs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Portrait and memoirs")]

In 1970, Gruzman was the subject of the winning entry for the [Archibald Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize"), painted by [Eric Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Smith_(artist) "Eric Smith (artist)").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-29) Gruzman sat for Smith several times, and commissioned Smith to contribute mosaics and stained glass for buildings he designed, including the South Head and District Synagogue in Rose Bay, as well as paintings Smith produced for the houses of his clients.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-31) Eric Smith later painted Gruzman's client and gallery owner [Rudy Komon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Komon "Rudy Komon") in 1981, again winning the [Archibald Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archibald_Prize "Archibald Prize").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-32)

Most of Gruzman's houses were photographed by [Max Dupain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Dupain "Max Dupain") and [David Moore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moore_(Australian_photographer) "David Moore (Australian photographer)").

Gruzman's memoirs, incorporated into a book written by [Philip Goad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Goad "Philip Goad") and featuring many of the Dupain and Moore photographs, was published posthumously in 2006 by Craftsman House.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-33)

## Honours

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Neville_Gruzman&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Honours")]

An exhibition of Gruzman's work was held at the [RAIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Institute_of_Architects "Australian Institute of Architects") NSW Chapter in 1983, and a retrospective was held in 1992 at the Rex Irwin Gallery in Sydney.

Gruzman was appointed a [Member of the Order of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_Australia "Member of the Order of Australia") (AM) in the 1985 Australia Day Honours.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-34)

The _Margot and Neville Gruzman Award for Urban Design in Architecture_ was named after Gruzman acknowledging his commitment to teaching of architecture and urban design at the [University of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_New_South_Wales "University of New South Wales"). The award is given to the best fourth year student, and an award for best final year architecture student whose design studio project best recognises the importance of urban design in architecture.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Gruzman#cite_note-keulemans-27)

# Council Flays Australian Mayor Who `would Not Work for Jews’

[February 20, 1996 See Original Daily Bulletin From This Date](http://pdfs.jta.org/1996/1996_02_20.pdf)

A Jewish-born mayor of a suburb near here has been censured by his own council after the release of a letter from 1992 in which he said he “wouldn’t work for Jewish clients.”

Mayor Neville Gruzman, who is a member of the Church of England, was booed and heckled at a recent meeting of the Woollahra Council as a result of the letter.

Jeffrey Hilton, a Jewish lawyer in Sydney who received the letter, said Gruzman had originally agreed to work for him because he has a non-Jewish wife, which, in Gruzman’s eyes, makes him a “better” Jew.

The council eventually decided, after a long and bitter debate, to give Gruzman one week “to show cause why he should not resign.”

Gruzman said his comments “were not made for any racist reason” but because he had difficulty in dealing with the “different ways of practicing” business that Jews use. He also said dealing with Jews could result in “aggravation.”

During the debate, the only Jewish member of the council, Julian Leeser, said Gruzman had made another anti-Jewish remark in an interview with a national television journalist.

Some council members defended Gruzman, saying that he was being attacked for political reasons.

The New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, which represents the jewish community in the area, has publicly criticized the mayor.

The head of the Orthodox Rabbinical Council of New South Wales, Rabbi Selwyn Franklin, had written to all the council members, arguing that “one who has expressed such views should not be entitled to hold public office in Australia.”

The council represents an area where a number of Jews reside and several synagogues exist.

# Council Flays Australian Mayor Who `would Not Work for Jews’

[February 20, 1996 See Original Daily Bulletin From This Date](http://pdfs.jta.org/1996/1996_02_20.pdf)

A Jewish-born mayor of a suburb near here has been censured by his own council after the release of a letter from 1992 in which he said he “wouldn’t work for Jewish clients.”

Mayor Neville Gruzman, who is a member of the Church of England, was booed and heckled at a recent meeting of the Woollahra Council as a result of the letter.

Jeffrey Hilton, a Jewish lawyer in Sydney who received the letter, said Gruzman had originally agreed to work for him because he has a non-Jewish wife, which, in Gruzman’s eyes, makes him a “better” Jew.

The council eventually decided, after a long and bitter debate, to give Gruzman one week “to show cause why he should not resign.”

Gruzman said his comments “were not made for any racist reason” but because he had difficulty in dealing with the “different ways of practicing” business that Jews use. He also said dealing with Jews could result in “aggravation.”

During the debate, the only Jewish member of the council, Julian Leeser, said Gruzman had made another anti-Jewish remark in an interview with a national television journalist.

Some council members defended Gruzman, saying that he was being attacked for political reasons.

The New South Wales Jewish Board of Deputies, which represents the jewish community in the area, has publicly criticized the mayor.

The head of the Orthodox Rabbinical Council of New South Wales, Rabbi Selwyn Franklin, had written to all the council members, arguing that “one who has expressed such views should not be entitled to hold public office in Australia.”

The council represents an area where a number of Jews reside and several synagogues exist.

This **timeline of Australian television** lists important [station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_station "Television station") launches, [programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_program "Television program"), major television events, and technological advancements that have significantly changed the forms of [broadcasting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_broadcasting_in_Australia "Television broadcasting in Australia") available to viewers of television in Australia. The [history of television in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_in_Australia#History "Television in Australia") can be traced back to an announcement from the [Menzies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Menzies "Robert Menzies")' government concerning plans for television services in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") and [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His50-1)

The new [medium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Media_of_Australia "Media of Australia") was introduced by [Bruce Gyngell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Gyngell "Bruce Gyngell") with the words _"Good evening, and welcome to television"_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-50Years-2)[Colour television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television#Color_television "History of television") was introduced in 1975, while [subscription television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pay_television "Pay television"), initially on the [Galaxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_(Australian_television) "Galaxy (Australian television)") platform, began in the mid-1990s. [Digital terrestrial television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_television_in_Australia "Digital television in Australia") was introduced on 1 January 2001 in Australia's five largest capital cities, later to be expanded to smaller cities and regional areas.

## 1920s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: 1920s")]

*   Experimental TV broadcasts began as early as 1929 in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") on stations [3DB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3TTT "3TTT") and [3UZ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3UZ "3UZ") using the _Radiovision_ system by Gilbert Miles and Donal McDonald.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-3)
*   Thomas (Tom) M. B. Elliott experiments with an electromechanical version of television using the Nipkow disc technique that [Baird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Logie_Baird "John Logie Baird") employed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-4)

## 1930s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1930s")]

*   Other experimental transmissions followed in other cities, such as the 30 line [Baird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Logie_Baird "John Logie Baird") system in [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane") in 1934[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-Cour34-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-Lee-6) by Tom Elliott and Dr Val McDowall, members of the Royal Society of Queensland, at the amateur station (VK)4CM.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-8) By 1938 Elliot demonstrated an electronic 180 line version.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-Lee-6)

## 1940s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1940s")]

*   Broadcasting tests halted due to the advent of World War 2.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-Lee-6)

## 1950s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1950s")]

1950
*   June: [Robert Menzies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Menzies "Robert Menzies")' government announces a gradual introduction of [television in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_in_Australia "Television in Australia"), with plans to launch an [ABC Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australia) "ABC Television (Australia)") station in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") and other areas subject to funding approval. As well as this, commercial television services in Sydney and [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") are planned with _"any other capital city where it is felt that the applicant's capacity to provide a service justifies the issue of a licence"._[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-cabinet-9)

1953
*   January: The Menzies government amends the _1948 Broadcasting Act_ to provide legislative framework for commercial television licenses.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-smh-10)

1954
*   The [Royal Commission on Television](http://nla.gov.au/nla.obj-348722997/view?partId=nla.obj-348726639#page/n26/mode/1up) affirms the need to introduce television under a dual system of ownership, similarly to the [Menzies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Menzies "Robert Menzies") plan.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-11)

1956
*   13 July: Test transmissions commence in Sydney on TCN-9 in monochrome.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-first24-12)
*   16 July: HSV-7 Melbourne commences test transmissions in monochrome.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-13)
*   16 September: [TCN-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCN "TCN") Sydney launches at 7.00pm. Announcer John Godson is the first voice heard and [Bruce Gyngell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Gyngell "Bruce Gyngell") is the first person seen in-vision, introducing _This is Television_.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-birth-14)
*   27 October: TCN-9 officially opens.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-first24-12)
*   4 November: [HSV-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSV_(TV_station) "HSV (TV station)")[Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") officially launches.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His50-1)
*   5 November: The [Australian Broadcasting Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Australian Broadcasting Corporation") begins television broadcasting with [ABN-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABN_(TV_station) "ABN (TV station)") Sydney.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-birth-14)
*   19 November: ABV-2 Melbourne launches
*   22 November: [1956 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1956_Summer_Olympics "1956 Summer Olympics") in Melbourne commence, televised by ABV-2 & HSV-7 and during [GTV-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTV_(Australia) "GTV (Australia)") test transmissions.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-heritage-15)
*   2 December: [ATN-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATN-7 "ATN-7") officially opens.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-first24-12)

1957
*   19 January: Sir Dallas Brookes officially inaugurates [GTV-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTV-9 "GTV-9") Melbourne.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His50-1)
*   6 May: [GTV-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTV-9 "GTV-9") launches the nightly variety show _[In Melbourne Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_Melbourne\_Tonight "In Melbourne Tonight")_ with [Graham Kennedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graham_Kennedy "Graham Kennedy").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-16)

1959
*   9 January: Melbourne and Sydney are linked by [microwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microwave "Microwave") for the first time, allowing programs to be broadcast live to both cities concurrently.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-heritage-15)
*   1 July: _[Mr. Squiggle and Friends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Squiggle\_and\_Friends "Mr. Squiggle and Friends")_ begins on ABC.
*   16 August: [QTQ-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QTQ "QTQ")[Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane") begins transmission.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-qtq-17)
*   5 September: [NWS-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWS_(TV_station) "NWS (TV station)")[Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide "Adelaide") officially launches.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-nws-18)
*   16 October: [TVW-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVW "TVW")[Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth") launches.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-seven50s-19)
*   24 October: [ADS-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADS "ADS") Adelaide launches.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-ads-20)
*   1 November: [BTQ-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BTQ "BTQ") Brisbane launches.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-seven50s-19)
*   2 November: [ABQ-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABQ "ABQ") Brisbane launches.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)

## 1960s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1960s")]

1960
*   11 March: [ABS-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABS_(TV_station) "ABS (TV station)")[Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide "Adelaide") launches.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)
*   7 May: [ABW-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABW_(TV_station) "ABW (TV station)")[Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth") begins transmission.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)
*   23 May: [TVT-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVT_(TV_station) "TVT (TV station)")[Hobart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart "Hobart") opens, bringing television to Tasmania.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)
*   4 June: [ABT-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABT_(TV_station) "ABT (TV station)") Hobart commences broadcasting.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)

1961
*   19 August: Current affairs program _[Four Corners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four\_Corners\_(Australian\_TV\_program) "Four Corners (Australian TV program)")_ begins on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-22)
*   9 December: [GLV-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLV/BCV "GLV/BCV")[Traralgon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traralgon,_Victoria "Traralgon, Victoria") is the first regional station to open.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sc10vic-23)
*   23 December: [BCV-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLV/BCV "GLV/BCV") launches in [Bendigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bendigo "Bendigo") while [GMV-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTV_(TV_station) "VTV (TV station)") began in [Shepparton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shepparton,_Victoria "Shepparton, Victoria").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sc10vic-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-winvic-24)

1962
*   4 March: [NBN-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBN_Television "NBN Television")[Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle,_New_South_Wales "Newcastle, New South Wales") begins broadcasting.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-25)
*   17 March: [CBN-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBN_(Australian_TV_station) "CBN (Australian TV station)")[Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange,_New_South_Wales "Orange, New South Wales") launches.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)
*   18 March: [WIN-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WIN_Television "WIN Television")[Wollongong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wollongong "Wollongong") begins.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-winsnsw-27)
*   27 April: [BTV-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTV_(TV_station) "VTV (TV station)")[Ballarat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballarat "Ballarat") begins transmission.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-winvic-24)
*   12 May: [RTN-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTN-8 "RTN-8")[Lismore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lismore,_New_South_Wales "Lismore, New South Wales") begins broadcasting.
*   26 May: [TNT-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_(Australian_TV_station) "TNT (Australian TV station)") begins transmission to [Launceston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Launceston,_Tasmania "Launceston, Tasmania") and northern [Tasmania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tasmania "Tasmania").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-wintas-28)
*   2 June: [CTC-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CTC_(TV_station) "CTC (TV station)")[Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra "Canberra") officially commences transmissions.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sc10snsw-29)
*   1 July: [Frank Packer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Packer "Frank Packer") (owner of TCN-9 Sydney) buys GTV-9 Melbourne, forming the [National Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network"), the first in the country.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   13 July: [DDQ-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTQ "RTQ")[Toowoomba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toowoomba "Toowoomba") begins transmission.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-winqld-31)
*   1 November: [TNQ-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNQ "TNQ") launches in [Townsville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Townsville "Townsville").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sevenqld-32)
*   18 December: [ABC-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_(TV_station) "ABC (TV station)") Canberra launches.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-abc50s60s-21)

1963
*   7 September: [RTQ-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RTQ-7 "RTQ-7")[Rockhampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockhampton "Rockhampton") begins broadcasting.

1964
*   19 June: [RVN-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMV_(TV_station) "AMV (TV station)")[Wagga Wagga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wagga_Wagga "Wagga Wagga") launches.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)
*   1 August: [ATV-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATV_(Australia) "ATV (Australia)"), [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne")'s third commercial station, launches.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   7 September: [AMV-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMV_(TV_station) "AMV (TV station)")[Albury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albury,_New_South_Wales "Albury, New South Wales") commences broadcasting.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)

1965
*   23 January: [NRN-11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRN-11 "NRN-11")[Coffs Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffs_Harbour "Coffs Harbour") begins broadcasting.
*   5 April: [TEN-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TEN_(TV_station) "TEN (TV station)")[Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") begins transmission.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-tensyd-33)
*   10 April: [WBQ-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STQ "STQ")[Wide Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_of_Wide_Bay "Division of Wide Bay")/[Maryborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryborough,_Queensland "Maryborough, Queensland")[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sevenqld-32) and [NEN-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEN_(TV_station) "NEN (TV station)")[Tamworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamworth,_New_South_Wales "Tamworth, New South Wales") begin transmission.
*   12 May: [NRN-11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRN "NRN")[Coffs Harbour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coffs_Harbour "Coffs Harbour") begins broadcasting.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sc10nnsw-34)
*   12 June: [STW-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STW "STW")[Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth") opens.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-stw-35)
*   1 July: [TVQ-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVQ "TVQ")[Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane") launches.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-tenbris-36)
*   26 July: [SAS-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAS_(TV_station) "SAS (TV station)")[Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide "Adelaide") launches.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-tenbris-36)
*   27 September: [NEN-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEN_(TV_station) "NEN (TV station)")[Tamworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamworth,_New_South_Wales "Tamworth, New South Wales") begins transmission.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)
*   27 November: [STV-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VTV_(TV_station) "VTV (TV station)")[Mildura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mildura "Mildura") launches.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-winvic-24)
*   1 December: Australia's first regional television network is formed when [CWN-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBN_(Australian_TV_station) "CBN (Australian TV station)")[Dubbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubbo "Dubbo") opens as a direct relay of CBN-8 Orange.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)
*   15 December: [MTN-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTN_(TV_station) "MTN (TV station)")[Griffith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Griffith,_New_South_Wales "Griffith, New South Wales") commences transmission.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)

1966
*   25 March: [SES-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SES/RTS "SES/RTS")[Mount Gambier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Gambier,_South_Australia "Mount Gambier, South Australia") officially launches.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   18 July: _[Play School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Play\_School\_(Australian\_TV\_series) "Play School (Australian TV series)")_ begins on ABC
*   27 May: [ECN-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEN_(TV_station) "NEN (TV station)")[Taree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taree,_New_South_Wales "Taree, New South Wales") launches.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-prime60s-26)
*   7 September: [FNQ-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNQ "TNQ") begins transmission in and around [Cairns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairns "Cairns").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sc10qld-37)

1967
*   10 March: [BTW-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_West_Network "Golden West Network")[Bunbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunbury,_Western_Australia "Bunbury, Western Australia") becomes the first regional television station in [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-gwn-38)
*   10 April: [ABC TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)") current affairs program _[This Day Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Day\_Tonight "This Day Tonight")_ premieres.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   15 June: Test [colour television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_television#Color_television "History of television") transmissions are made for the first time in Australia by ATV-0.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)

1968
*   [TVW-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TVW "TVW") conducts its first [Telethon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telethon "Telethon").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   1 March: [GTS-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTS-4 "GTS-4")[Port Pirie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Pirie,_South_Australia "Port Pirie, South Australia") launches.
*   9 August: [MVQ-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STQ "STQ") launches in [Mackay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mackay,_Queensland "Mackay, Queensland").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sevenqld-32)
*   16 August: [BKN-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GTS/BKN "GTS/BKN")[Broken Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broken_Hill,_New_South_Wales "Broken Hill, New South Wales") opens.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-gwn-38)

1969
*   20 July: The [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") Moon landing is televised live by [television stations in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Television_broadcasting_in_Australia "Television broadcasting in Australia").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-first24-12)

*   Undated: First fully colour capable production facility opened in Sydney (Video Tape Corp, in East Roseville).

## 1970s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1970s")]

1971
*   4 January: Long running US children's educational series _[Sesame Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sesame\_Street "Sesame Street")_ begins on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)").
*   18 June: [VEW-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_West_Network "Golden West Network")[Kalgoorlie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalgoorlie "Kalgoorlie") begins broadcasting.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-39)
*   13 August: [ABD-6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABD_(TV_station) "ABD (TV station)") launches as [Darwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darwin,_Northern_Territory "Darwin, Northern Territory")'s first television station.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His60-30)
*   11 September: [ITQ-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/QQQ "QQQ")[Mount Isa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Isa "Mount Isa") begins broadcasting.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-sccentral-40)
*   9 October: _[Hey Hey It's Saturday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey\_Hey\_It's\_Saturday "Hey Hey It's Saturday")_ starts off as a Saturday morning cartoon program for children on [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network").
*   22 November: _[A Current Affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Current\_Affair\_(Australian\_TV\_series) "A Current Affair (Australian TV series)")_, hosted by [Mike Willesee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Willesee "Mike Willesee"), makes its first appearance on the [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His70-41)
*   11 November: [NTD-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTD_(Australian_TV_station) "NTD (Australian TV station)") is officially launched by [Administrator of the Northern Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrator_of_the_Northern_Territory "Administrator of the Northern Territory"), [Fred Chaney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fred_Chaney "Fred Chaney").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-42)

1972
*   13 March: Soap opera _[Number 96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number\_96\_(TV\_series) "Number 96 (TV series)")_ debuts, heralding the night 'Australian television lost its virginity'
*   20 March: Brisbane channel [BTQ-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BTQ "BTQ") claims Australia's first one-hour news bulletin, The Big News[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His70-41)

1973
*   In 1973, the only Australian designed and made precision colour television monitor,was produced for local use and international export. The broadcast quality monitor (LDN5006)was developed by Willem Sparrius, Project Engineer at Philips subsidiary company Electronics Engineering Communications and produced at their South Oakleigh plant.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-DoubleDutch-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-OakleighWorldHeadquarters-44)

1974
*   29 August: [GSW-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_West_Network "Golden West Network")[Albany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albany,_Western_Australia "Albany, Western Australia") begins broadcasting as a relay of VEW-8 Kalgoorlie.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
*   October: Colour test transmissions begin on Australian television.
*   8 November: _[Countdown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Countdown\_(Australian\_TV\_series) "Countdown (Australian TV series)")_ begins on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)").

1975
*   1 March: At midnight, [colour television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colour_television "Colour television") is introduced across the country. The main networks celebrate with their own unique slogan – _Come to Colour_ (ABC TV), _Seven Colors Your World_ (Seven Network), _Living Color_ (Nine Network) and _0 – First in Color_ (0-10 Network).[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-birth-14)

1976
*   26 November: [RTS-5A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SES/RTS "SES/RTS") Loxton launches in the [Riverland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riverland "Riverland") district.

1977
*   21 January: [GTW-11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_West_Network "Golden West Network")[Geraldton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geraldton "Geraldton") begins broadcasting, completing the roll-out of regional commercial television across Australia.
*   24 September: The _[Victorian Football League Grand Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian\_Football\_League#Premiership\_season "Australian Football League")_ is broadcast live to viewers in [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") for the first time.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His70-41)

1979
*   11 February: Current affairs program _[60 Minutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60\_Minutes\_(Australian\_TV\_program) "60 Minutes (Australian TV program)")_ debuts on the [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network").
*   7 April: The [Special Broadcasting Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Broadcasting_Service "Special Broadcasting Service") begins test transmissions on [ABV-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABV_(TV_station) "ABV (TV station)")[Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne") and [ABN-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABN_(TV_station) "ABN (TV station)")[Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), with foreign-language programming shown on Sunday mornings.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His70-41)

## 1980s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Timeline_of_Australian_television&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1980s")]

1980
*   20 January: [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne,_Australia "Melbourne, Australia")'s [ATV-0](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATV-0 "ATV-0") converts to [ATV-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ATV-10 "ATV-10"); after nearby La Trobe Valley regional station GLV-10 converts to [GLV-8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLV/BCV "GLV/BCV") to facilitate this change, which concurrently frees up the frequency for [Channel 0/28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)") later that same year.
*   14 July: Game show _[Sale of the Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sale\_of\_the\_Century\_(Australian\_game\_show) "Sale of the Century (Australian game show)")_ debuts on the [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network").
*   24 October: [Channel 0/28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)") is launched by [Bruce Gyngell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Gyngell "Bruce Gyngell") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") and [Melbourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne "Melbourne").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-birth-14)

1982
*   28 June: The [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network") Australia premieres _[Today](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Today\_(1982\_TV\_program) "Today (1982 TV program)")_.

1983
*   1 July: The Australian Broadcasting Commission becomes the [Australian Broadcasting Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Australian Broadcasting Corporation").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-whoseabc-45)
*   16 October: Channel 0/28 expands into [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra "Canberra"), [Cooma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooma,_New_South_Wales "Cooma, New South Wales") and [Goulburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goulburn,_New_South_Wales "Goulburn, New South Wales"), and changes its name to [Network 0-28](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)

1984
*   4 February: _[Hey Hey It's Saturday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hey\_Hey\_It's\_Saturday "Hey Hey It's Saturday")_ moves from its morning timeslot to the 9.30 pm timeslot.
*   July: The [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") are broadcast on [Network Ten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Ten "Network Ten").
*   26 July: US-French-Canadian animated series _[Inspector Gadget](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspector\_Gadget\_(1983\_TV\_series) "Inspector Gadget (1983 TV series)")_ begins on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Australian Broadcasting Corporation").

1985
*   18 February: Network 0-28 once again changes its name to [SBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_(Australian_TV_channel) "SBS (Australian TV channel)"), and begins daytime transmissions.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)
*   4 March: _ABC National_, a one-hour national news and current affairs program shown from 6.30 pm, replaces [ABC TV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)")'s half-hour 7.00pm state news bulletins.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-whoseabc-45)
*   18 March: Soap opera _[Neighbours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neighbours "Neighbours")_ begins on the [Seven Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Network "Seven Network").
*   30 June: [SBS Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SBS_Television "SBS Television") expands into [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane"), [Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide "Adelaide"), [Newcastle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle,_New_South_Wales "Newcastle, New South Wales"), [Wollongong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wollongong "Wollongong"), and the [Gold Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast,_Queensland "Gold Coast, Queensland").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)
*   24 October: The [ABC Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation#Management "Australian Broadcasting Corporation") elects to abandon _ABC National_.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-whoseabc-45)

1986
*   5 January: SBS Television phases out its second [VHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Very_high_frequency "Very high frequency") 0 channel.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)
*   16 March: SBS launches in [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth") and [Hobart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hobart "Hobart").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)
*   19 August: [Treasurer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasurer_of_Australia "Treasurer of Australia")[Paul Keating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Keating "Paul Keating"), in his budget speech, announces the amalgamation of the [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Australian Broadcasting Corporation") and [SBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Broadcasting_Service "Special Broadcasting Service").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-whoseabc-45)

1987
*   26 March: [Bob Hawke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Hawke "Bob Hawke") calls off the proposed amalgamation of the ABC and SBS.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-whoseabc-45)
*   17 April: _[Rage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rage\_(TV\_program) "Rage (TV program)")_ begins on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Television_(Australian_TV_network) "ABC Television (Australian TV network)").
*   27 December: [Adelaide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide "Adelaide") stations SAS-10 and ADS-7 swap frequencies to become [SAS-7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAS_(TV_station) "SAS (TV station)") and [ADS-10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADS_(TV_station) "ADS (TV station)").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Australian_television#cite_note-His80-46)

1988
*   1 January: [Nine Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Network "Nine Network") first use of SNG (Satellite News Gathering) in Australia. Transmission from Kingoonya SA for Australia Live 88 which showcased Australia remotely in a four hour broadcast.
*   2 January: [Imparja Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imparja_Television "Imparja Television") launches in remote eastern and central Australia from studios in [Alice Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Springs "Alice Springs").
